title: 北への武器 香港の密輸集団が暗躍
body:
米国で２０２４年に中国籍の男が摘発された対北朝鮮密輸事件で、自由貿易港の香港を拠点とする中国人らの民間人集団が介在していることが複数の関係者の証言でわかった。中継地の香港に送られた銃器類を北朝鮮に送るにあたっては、帰任する北朝鮮外交官の船便の荷物に紛れ込ませる巧妙な手法を用いていたことも判明した。北朝鮮の武器密輸に対する国際監視網が弱まる中、この密輸集団は現在も暗躍しているという。【図表】香港を拠点とする集団の対北朝鮮密輸の手口
関係者によると、香港からの密輸を主導したのは、米国からの荷受人となった「裕領貿易有限公司」の実質的経営者である蔡という姓の香港籍の男だった。
蔡という男は在香港北朝鮮総領事館の２３年の閉鎖に伴って帰任する外交官の家財輸送も請け負っていた。米国から２３年１２月に発送された武器の香港到着を待ち、手配していたシエラレオネ船籍（当時）の貨物船「サンリッチ」に一緒に積み込んだ。
武器は「冷蔵庫」「厨房（ちゅうぼう）用品」の名目で申告した。膨大な貨物が行き来する自由貿易港の香港は輸出入の手続きが簡素な上、税関当局が外交官の荷物を詳しく調べないと計算した上での偽装だった。外交官は事情を一切承知していなかったという。
関係者によると、密輸には、貨物船を事実上保有する王という姓の台湾籍の男、船舶運航会社「天馬船務有限公司」の実質的経営者である梁という姓の中国籍の男も関与していた。
関係者によると密輸集団は貨物船４隻態勢で活動を続けている。最近は、国連安全保障理事会決議に基づく制裁で北朝鮮輸出が禁じられている鉄鋼類の輸送が目立つほか、マレーシアから北朝鮮への石油の密輸を計画している可能性がある。
北朝鮮に対する制裁決議の履行状況を監視する国連安保理の北朝鮮制裁委員会・専門家パネルは、ロシアが任期延長決議案に拒否権を行使したことで、２４年４月末で活動停止を余儀なくされた。

title: スペイン事故 邦人1人の死亡確認
body: スペイン中部で10月28日に、列車同士が衝突して69人が死亡した事故で、スペイン当局は1日、日本人1人の死亡が確認されたと発表しました。【動画】時速200kmで追突可能性も…複数の“人為的ミス”が原因か現地の当局が設置した統合データセンターによりますと、1日までに死者69人のうち66人の身元が特定され、日本人1人が含まれていることが明らかになりました。名前は公表されていません。10月28日の事故直後、スペイン政府から｢追突した側の列車の乗客名簿に日本人2人の名前が載っている｣と日本政府に連絡があり、このうちの1人とみられます。身元が特定された66人の国籍の内訳はスペイン54人、アルゼンチン1人、カナダ1人、チェコ1人、アメリカ4人、フランス1人、日本1人、メキシコ1人、ポルトガル1人、チュニジア1人となっています。このうち60人についてはすでに家族への通知が完了しています。身元が特定されていない残りの死者3人については全員がスペイン以外の外国籍だとみられています。事故にあった列車に乗っていた可能性がある外国人のうち、現在、日本人1人、オーストラリア人2人の合わせて3人の安否が確認できていないということです。在スペイン日本大使館はスペイン当局の発表を受けて｢日本政府としてもスペイン当局と連携して身元の確認と家族の支援に全力で取り組む｣としています。列車の事故原因については信号システムの不具合や運行管理上の人為的なミスが指摘されていて、関係者の責任の有無を調べるため捜査が進められています。捜査当局は列車の運行記録が残る｢ブラックボックス｣を回収し、解析を進めるとともに関係者への事情聴取を通じて当時の運行手順が適切だったかどうか詳しく調べているとみられます。

title: 私立高の学校納付金2倍 NGO調査
body:
私立高校に通う生徒の家庭が負担する施設維持費や冷暖房費などの「学校納付金」の平均額が2026年度は約14万7千円で、約7万3千円だった25年度の約2倍となったことが2日までに分かった。非政府組織（NGO）「セーブ・ザ・チルドレン・ジャパン」が調査結果を公表した。26年度から私立も高校授業料無償化の対象となったが、回答した高1の27％は授業料以外の出費を懸念し「私立を選択肢に入れられなかった」とした。【画像】退学希望者が続出「幻滅大学」の酷すぎる実態　コロナで浮き彫りになった格差　20年
同団体が提供する給付金制度を利用した家庭を対象にアンケートを実施し、進学時にかかった費用などを尋ねた。中高生125人と保護者425人から回答があった。私立高の入学時にかかった他の主な費用の平均額は、入学金が25年度比約2万7千円増の約17万3千円、制服代が約1万5千円増の約10万8千円、パソコン・タブレット代が約8千円増の約9万9千円。子どもが私立高に通う保護者の約半数は「経済的な理由で就学を続けられない可能性がある」とした。

title: 結核上回る患者数 NTM症の対策
body:
結核を超える勢いで患者数が増加している呼吸器の感染症「NTM症（非結核性抗酸菌症）」。初期症状は風邪に似ており、経過が緩やかなことから見過ごされがちだが、進行すると肺機能が低下し、重篤な状態に陥ることもある。女性を中心に注意が必要とされるこの疾患について、専門医の解説や実際の患者の声をもとに、その実態と感染リスクを減らすための対策を解説する。【動画】「体重が10kg以上減り、何度も吐血…」水回りや土から感染するNTM症　初期症状と対策
全国的に患者数が増加傾向にある呼吸器の感染症「NTM症（肺非結核性抗酸菌症）」。患者数は2007年から2014年までの7年間で約2.6倍に増え、結核の患者数を上回っている。さらに死亡者数も2000年代前半から徐々に増加し、2019年ごろを境に結核による死亡者数を超えた。年代別ではほとんどの年代で女性の感染率が高く、特に60代や70代では女性が男性の2倍以上となっている。9月には厚生労働省が早期受診を呼びかける啓発活動を行うなど、社会的な警戒感が高まっている。しかし、街頭で話を聞くと、「聞いたことがない」「初めて知った」と答える人が多く、一般の認知度はまだ低いのが現状だ。
NTM症を引き起こす病原体は結核菌に近い仲間の細菌だが、結核とは異なり人から人へ感染することはない。愛泉会宮崎医療福祉センター　峰松俊夫医師:NTMはもともと環境中にいる細菌で、よくいるところは水とか土壌とか埃とか、そういった自然環境にいます。そういったところからたまたま人の体内に入ってきて、それが原因で発症するのがNTM症。気管支拡張症や慢性閉塞性肺疾患を患っている人、過去に肺結核を経験した人は肺にNTMの細菌の塊ができやすく、発症リスクが高まります。
宮崎市にある「かいクリニック呼吸器内科」の飯干医師は、患者の増加を肌で感じている。かいクリニック呼吸器内科　飯干宏俊医師:患者からNTM症についての問い合わせは度々あります。咳と痰が2週間以上続くのは、普通の風邪とは、急性期とは違うので、慢性的に2週間から4週間続くので、と来られる方が多いです。NTM症の初期症状は風邪と似ており、息切れ、胸の痛み、体のだるさ、37度台の微熱、血痰などがある。しかし特筆すべきは無症状の人が多いことで、感染した人の34％、実に3人に1人は無症状というデータが出ている。さらに、医師が警鐘を鳴らすのはその進行の遅さだ。かいクリニック呼吸器内科　飯干宏俊医師:結核は数か月ごとに広がっていくけど、非結核性抗酸菌症は知らずのうちに10年、20年かかって感染していることが分かってきます。治療のタイミングが遅れると、肺の機能が落ちてしまいます。愛泉会宮崎医療福祉センター　峰松俊夫医師:肺の広い範囲が障害されて呼吸不全になると、低酸素血症や大量の吐血が起こったりします。二次感染を起こして入院や在宅酸素療法が必要になるケースもあります。

title: ウクライナ南部の局地停戦が終了
body:
【キーウ、モスクワ共同】ロシアの占領下で孤立したウクライナ南部ヘルソン州オレシュキへの人道支援実施のため、両国間で合意した局地的な停戦が1日、期限を迎え終了した。両国の連携で支援や住民の退避が成功し、和平につながることが望まれるが、10月27日から約6日の期間中も他地域では攻撃が続いた。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
合意を仲介したトランプ米大統領の妻メラニアさんは、停戦で「住民は常に攻撃の恐れにさらされることなく、尊厳を取り戻した。オレシュキを持続的和平の出発点としよう」とX（旧ツイッター）で呼びかけた。ロシアのラントラトワ連邦人権問題全権代表は「オレシュキは第一歩となるべきだ」とし、戦闘の前線周辺で暮らす人々への支援実施に意欲を表明。一方、停戦の対象となったヘルソン方面以外では、1日もロシアの無人機などによる攻撃が続き、地元当局によると西部ビンニツァ州、北東部スムイ州で計3人が死亡した。ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領は1日、ロシア南部ロストフ州のコンビナートに長距離攻撃を行ったとXで明らかにした。

title: ハロウィン繁華街で銃撃相次ぐ 米
body: （CNN）　ハロウィーンを楽しむ人たちでにぎわう米テキサス州ダラスの繁華街で11月1日未明、3件の銃撃事件が相次ぎ、警察によると4人が死亡、約15人が負傷した。銃撃事件はいずれもダラスのダウンタウン東部にある繁華街ディープエラム地区で発生。この日は複数のライブハウスがハロウィーンのイベントを宣伝していた。ダラス警察のこれまでの捜査によると、1日午前0時20分ごろに最初の銃撃事件が発生。続いて同1時過ぎと、その約30分後に続けて発生した。警察は銃撃犯の特定を急いでおり、複数の人物を逮捕して事情を聴いている。事件との関係は現時点で分かっていないという。この地区の飲食店に勤務するブライ・ジェイソンさんは、その日の勤務を終えた後も繁華街にとどまっていたところ、最初の銃撃が始まったとCNNに証言。人々が悲鳴を上げながら逃げ惑うのを見たと話している。警察は、ハロウィーンの雑踏を見越して警官の配備を増やし、警戒を強めていたという。警官にけがはなかったとしている。ジェイソンさんによると、一帯のバーはどこも客であふれかえっていて、通りも人々がひしめき合う状態だった。「ここにはもう何年も前からいるけれど、こんなことに巻き込まれるのは到底初めてではない」とジェイソンさん。ここでは銃暴力が「ごく普通」の出来事になっていると言い添えた。被害者の身元や負傷者のけがの程度は1日午前の時点では明らかになっていない。

title: 北への武器 香港の密輸集団が暗躍
body:
米国で２０２４年に中国籍の男が摘発された対北朝鮮密輸事件で、自由貿易港の香港を拠点とする中国人らの民間人集団が介在していることが複数の関係者の証言でわかった。中継地の香港に送られた銃器類を北朝鮮に送るにあたっては、帰任する北朝鮮外交官の船便の荷物に紛れ込ませる巧妙な手法を用いていたことも判明した。北朝鮮の武器密輸に対する国際監視網が弱まる中、この密輸集団は現在も暗躍しているという。【図表】香港を拠点とする集団の対北朝鮮密輸の手口
関係者によると、香港からの密輸を主導したのは、米国からの荷受人となった「裕領貿易有限公司」の実質的経営者である蔡という姓の香港籍の男だった。
蔡という男は在香港北朝鮮総領事館の２３年の閉鎖に伴って帰任する外交官の家財輸送も請け負っていた。米国から２３年１２月に発送された武器の香港到着を待ち、手配していたシエラレオネ船籍（当時）の貨物船「サンリッチ」に一緒に積み込んだ。
武器は「冷蔵庫」「厨房（ちゅうぼう）用品」の名目で申告した。膨大な貨物が行き来する自由貿易港の香港は輸出入の手続きが簡素な上、税関当局が外交官の荷物を詳しく調べないと計算した上での偽装だった。外交官は事情を一切承知していなかったという。
関係者によると、密輸には、貨物船を事実上保有する王という姓の台湾籍の男、船舶運航会社「天馬船務有限公司」の実質的経営者である梁という姓の中国籍の男も関与していた。
関係者によると密輸集団は貨物船４隻態勢で活動を続けている。最近は、国連安全保障理事会決議に基づく制裁で北朝鮮輸出が禁じられている鉄鋼類の輸送が目立つほか、マレーシアから北朝鮮への石油の密輸を計画している可能性がある。
北朝鮮に対する制裁決議の履行状況を監視する国連安保理の北朝鮮制裁委員会・専門家パネルは、ロシアが任期延長決議案に拒否権を行使したことで、２４年４月末で活動停止を余儀なくされた。

title: 金型の無償保管 公取委勧告が急増
body: 部品製造などに使われる「金型」を、元請けの会社が下請け事業者に無償で保管させる行為をめぐり、公正取引委員会が、元請け側に対し下請法（現・中小受託取引適正化法）違反だとして勧告を出すケースが急増している。【海外の言いなりに】減り続ける日本の「金型」製造業への警告立場の弱い下請け事業者が、古い製品の金型であっても廃棄できずに無償保管を強いられやすい構図がある。専門家は「苦境にあえぐ中小企業を保護する姿勢を明確にしたいという狙いが公取委にある」と分析する。金型は、ペットボトルなどの身近な製品のほか、自動車や機械などの部品を大量生産する際に使われる。重さ1トンを超える巨大な金型もあり、保管にも広いスペースが必要になる。公取委は2023年3月、金型の無償保管をめぐって初の勧告を元請けの会社に出した。22年度の勧告は1件だったが、23年度は3件、24年度は9件、25年度は26件と急増。今年度も10月9日までに10件の勧告を出している。「不当な経済上の利益の提供要請の禁止」にあたるとして、保管にかかる費用の相当額を速やかに元請けの会社に支払うよう求めた。これまでの計49件の勧告を朝日新聞が分析したところ、無償保管を求められた下請けはのべ2132事業者で、保管させられた金型などは12万6千点を超えていた。公取委から勧告を受けた元請けの会社のなかには、30年以上前から下請けに金型を無償保管させていたり、金型の管理状況を把握するための棚卸し（在庫確認）を無償でさせていたりしたケースもあったという。なぜ下請け事業者に金型を無償で保管させる事例が相次ぐのか。元請け側のメーカー会社などは、製品の修理に備えて部品を確保しておく必要がある。中小企業庁の調査では、無償保管のために新たに土地を購入したり、借りたりする下請け事業者もいたといい、下請け事業者が不当な負担を強いられている現状が浮かぶ。公取委で強制調査を担う犯則審査部の部長を務めた、神奈川大学名誉教授の細田孝一さんは「金型の無償保管の問題は昔からあったが、公取委は『不当な値引き』など、より悪質な行為への対応を優先してきた」と話す。一方で、近年は製造業の経営環境が悪化し、中小企業の廃業が相次ぐ。細田さんは「勧告の急増は、中小企業の利益を守るという公取委のメッセージだ」と指摘している。（浜田知宏）

title: 出国時に返金 新免税制度が開始
body: 訪日外国人客（インバウンド）を対象にした消費税の新たな免税制度が11月1日から始まった。店頭で消費税込みの価格で販売し、出国時に消費税分を返金する「リファンド（返金）方式」に変更する。免税品の不正転売対策が目的。現行の免税制度が1952年に導入されてから約74年ぶりの抜本改革となる。【図解でみる】免税品の不正転売、どう防ぐ?10月末までの旧方式では、旅行客が街中の免税店で5000円以上の商品を買った際、パスポートを提示すれば消費税抜きの価格で購入でき、出国時に税関が確認する方式を取っていた。ただ、免税品を国外に持ち出さずに日本国内で転売して、消費税分の利ざやを稼ぐ行為が相次いでいた。新方式では、免税店で旅行客が税込み価格で購入する。出国時に免税店で提示したパスポートを専用端末や専用ウェブサイトで照合。必要に応じて税関が免税品を所持しているか確認する。その後、クレジットカードや現金などで消費税分が返金されるが、免税品が確認できないと返金されない。新方式では、衣類や家電などの一般物品と食品などの消耗品の区分をやめ、消耗品に設けている1日1店舗当たり50万円の購入上限額も撤廃する。免税品を指定袋で特殊包装する必要もなくなる。【妹尾直道】

title: 内定者2年間入社しなくてOK 狙い
body: 新卒採用で企業から内定が出た学生は、大学（大学院）を卒業した翌月の4月に入社するのが一般的だ。だが、そんな「あたり前」を変えようとする企業がある。化粧品会社「シロ」は2028年度の新卒採用から「インターバル採用」という新制度を導入し、内定者は卒業後2年間のうち入社時期を自由に選ぶことができるようにする。なぜ卒業後に「間（インターバル）」を設けるのか。制度を考案した社長に“真意”を聞いた。【写真】入社時期は自由…「インターバル採用」を始めた企業の社長はこちら＊　　＊　　＊「海外留学でも、アルバイトでも、趣味に没頭してもOKです。逆に、何もせずにゆっくりするのでもいい。最大2年間は自由に何をして過ごしてもらっても構いません。その2年間で別のやりたいことが見つかれば、弊社の内定を辞退してもいいんです」化粧品ブランドSHIROを展開する「シロ」の福永敬弘社長はこう話す。同社は2028年に卒業する学生を対象とした採用活動から、入社時期を自由に選ぶことができる「インターバル採用」を始める。卒業から最大2年間は内定を保持したまま、自由に過ごすことができるという制度で、福永社長自らが考案した。企業側は内定者の連絡先は把握するが、どこで何をしているのかをたずねることはしないという。だがこの制度、企業側にどんなメリットがあるのか。せっかく費用をかけて採用活動をしてもそれが「水の泡」になる可能性もある。福永氏に制度の目的をたずねると「離職者を減らしたいからです」と話す。「かつて離職する社員にその理由を聞くと『実は海外留学をしてみたかった』『資格試験に挑戦してみたかった』など、本来やりたかったことをできなかったために会社を離れる決断をしたという声をたくさん聞いたんです。自分のやりたいことにフタをしたまま働いていると、ストレスも感じやすい。その結果、離職につながってしまう事例が多かった。だからこそ、やりたいことに没頭したり、自分の好きなものに向き合ったりする時間を過ごしてから入社してもらう。そのほうが離職者も減るのではないかと考えました」

title: みんなで大家さん 悔やむ出資者も
body:
高利回りをアピールして約２０００億円を集めた不動産投資商品「みんなで大家さん」を運用・販売する２社が事業許可取り消しの行政処分を受け、出資者の間で憤りや困惑が広がっている。１９９５年に制度化された不動産特定共同事業で取り消し処分は初めて。３万人を超える出資者の多くは出資金返還の見通しが立っていない。（木村誠、千葉支局　本田麻紘）【図解】一目でわかる…「みんなで大家さん」の構図
「出資金の返金はもう諦めるしかないのか」。「みんなで大家さん」に計１６００万円を出資した福岡市の女性（５３）は、途方に暮れている。
資金をつぎ込んだのは、不動産会社「共生バンク」（東京）が千葉県成田市の成田空港周辺で行う開発事業の土地に１口１００万円で投資する商品。グループ内の「都市綜研インベストファンド」（大阪）が不動産の管理・運営、「みんなで大家さん販売」（東京）が商品の販売を担った。
東京ドーム約１０個分の土地にホテルや展示場などを建設する計画で、２０２０年に年利７％をうたって販売が始まった。
利率の高さにひかれた女性は２３年、１２００万円を出資。配当を毎月数万円ずつ受け取り、２４年には別の不動産を対象とした商品にも４００万円を出資したが、昨年７月に突然、配当がストップしたという。
出資金の大半が戻らない恐れがあるのは、計１０００万円を出資した神奈川県の男性（４４）も同じだ。「今思えば集めた金をどう使うのか具体的な説明はなかった。もう少し調べて出資すればよかった」と悔やむ。
「みんなで大家さん」に何があったのか。開発工事の内容を示す開発登録簿によると、成田での土地開発は「２１年３月」に造成工事が完了する予定だったが、繰り返し延期された。昨年１１月には、用地の一部を貸していた成田国際空港会社との土地の賃貸借契約も終了し、工事は止まった。
２４年６月には、ファンド社など２社が出資者に対し、成田市の開発許可を得ていると説明していた土地の一部が許可の対象外だったなどとして、大阪府や東京都から３０日間の業務一部停止処分を受けた。海外での資金調達を目指したが難航し、ファンド社は今年７月２８日付で、２８００億円超の債務超過になったと府に報告。保有する土地・建物の評価額を自ら８分の１の約４００億円に下げた。

title: 望月衣塑子記者の対談本 回収へ
body: 朝日新聞出版は1日、東京新聞記者の望月衣塑子氏と思想家の内田樹氏の共著で9月に刊行した新書「常識なき世界を生き延びるために」の回収を決めたと発表した。2日以降、書店などに協力を依頼し、順次、回収作業に入るという。【写真】キャップにTシャツ姿で取材する東京新聞の望月衣塑子記者同書は2人の対談本で「日本中学生新聞」を創刊した高校生、川中だいじさんを取り上げた。川中さんに関する望月氏の発言部分で「川中くんは周りの子から『老害』と言われたり」との記述や、川中さんが小学生のころに張り出した壁新聞を先生にはがされたというエピソードなど4カ所の誤りがあったという。望月氏はX（旧ツイッター）で「川中さんについて事実と異なる記述を公表してしまい、深くお詫び申し上げます」と謝罪していた。同社によると書店の在庫など約8000部を回収する。ただ、2万部を発行しており、すでに購入された分についての対応は今後検討するという。

title: Ukraine air raid app apparently hacked as users receive false radiation threat, Air Force says
summary: Authorities say there is no threat and have advised the public to stay calm and follow official channels for information.
body:
Ukrainians are used to reacting to the warnings of Russian attacks sent via the air alert app
Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
The alerts, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with the first reading: "Radiation threat.  Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyivalerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
In a separate post on Telegram, the Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said that due to the Air Alert application, the Radiation Hazard signal was played on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region, and added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources
Several governors of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the oblast in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The governor of Vinnytsia oblast, Natalya Zabolotna said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry had earlier said the app was temporarily disabled for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised". It urged residents to turn on their smartphones' emergency notifications so they could receive state-issued distress signals.
The alerts occurred just minutes before the end of alocalised ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday and officially ended at 23:00 Sunday.
Fighting had continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place, to allow civilians toevacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
summary: A rare humanitarian ceasefire allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
body:
Emergency responders at the scene of a strike on Ukraine's Vinnytsia region
A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicatedits need for Patriot missiles- the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
Watch: Evacuees from Oleshky reunited with their families
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

title: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
summary: The move by Haley Stevens, who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, was called a "despicable betrayal" by one top Democrat.
body:
Haley Stevens, a sitting Democratic congresswoman, appeared alongside the Republican Senate candidate on Sunday
A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."
"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election, with one calling it a "despicable betrayal".
The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days.
Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.
Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead.
"This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.
When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing.
"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."
GUIDE: What are the US midterms?
EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms
IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope
The Michigan Senate race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in Tuesday's midterm elections. It is one of a handful of battleground contests that will ultimately decide control of the Senate.
The seat is currently held by a retiring Democrat and the last time a Republican was elected to this Senate seat was in 1994. But in presidential elections, it is one of the crucial swing states - Michigan voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.
Rogers welcomed Stevens' endorsement and said it showed "courage" during brief remarks with reporters.
President Donald Trump echoed that sentiment during a campaign rally in Iowa, calling her "very brave".
"I don't know Haley. I've never met Haley. But Haley said what few people were willing to say," Trump said. "I'd love her to join the Republican Party actually."
Many of Stevens' staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement, while the chair of the Democratic Party in Michigan said her decision "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about".
"We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Curtis Hertel said in a statement.
Top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer called Stevens' endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal".
What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
In downtown Detroit, several Democrats the BBC spoke to said they were disappointed by Stevens' endorsement of Rogers.
"I just genuinely don't understand it," she said. "I do think it's a betrayal of the party because the things she stands for are not the same things that he stands for as a Republican."
"Maybe she had frustrations with the party," Matthew Barera, another Michigan voter, said.
Others, including Republicans who support Rogers, said they doubted it would make a difference to the race.
"People can see right through her actions, you know? She's just angry," Marissa Lee, a Rogers supporter, told the BBC. "She is not going to make anybody change their mind."
Over the weekend, as Stevens' criticism of El-Sayed escalated, a number of Democratic politicians in Michigan publicly encouraged her to end the feud and back the party's candidates more directly.
After a bruising and sometimes bitter campaign earlier this year, El-Sayed, a left-wing outsider, defeated Stevens, the establishment-backed congresswoman, to win the party's nomination for the US Senate race.
The primary, and the pair's subsequent feud, has underlined divisions over the party's direction ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Former public health official El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants, has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel.
Stevens is a more centrist Democrat - and had the support of party figures such as Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer during the primary race.
The party is hoping to regain control of the Senate in Tuesday's elections, but will need a net gain of four seats to do so. A loss in Michigan - which they currently hold - would represent a major blow and leave them needing to flip five seats.

title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
summary: Five officers from the Hamas-run police have been killed in Khan Younis and three people, including a child, killed in Gaza City, officials say.
body:
Mourners attend the funeral of five Palestinians, who were killed in an Israeli strike
Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.
In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel.
"My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"
At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.
Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.
The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
summary: There were hundreds of arrests as protesters took to the streets in cities across France for the third weekend in a row.
body:
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
Police officers hit with Molotov cocktails during Paris protest
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests alsotook place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto hack
summary: The exchange froze transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
body:
Binance customers withdrew more than $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday followinga record hack last week.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), haveaccused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber attack, which is said to be the largest hack in history.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, but that the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", Binance posted on X.
It added that withdrawals for major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it has not been affected by the issue.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The crypto withdrawn represents just a fraction of the total value of assets held by Binance.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets in its custody.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

title: Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules
summary: New affordability checks mean you could be blocked from using Buy Now Pay Later but here are ways to avoid it.
body:
If you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it.
BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July.
This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay.
If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation.
BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppersmore access to refunds and independent rulingson complaints if things go wrong.
But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time.
There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed.
But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight.
Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media.
Slow down your purchases:is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it?
Be more careful about what you buyto avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizes
Cancel subscriptionsto escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous payments
Talk to debt charitiesfor help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentials
If you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control.
The government-backed, independent,MoneyHelper website,externalhas a guide to findingfree debt advice near you,external.
It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money.
There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, anda bill prioritiser,externalto show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment.
You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds.

title: Thousands of jobs at Virgin Media O2 to be cut
summary: The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be axed but it will likely be a sizeable chunk of its workforce, the BBC understands.
body:
Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff face redundancy risk as the telecoms firm looks to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition.
The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000 workforce, the BBC understands.
VMO2 has billions of debt on its balance sheet and is tackling competition from both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, a move which VMO2 has firmly opposed.
VMO2 declined to comment. The Prospect union, which represents VMO2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling".
Deputy general secretary Noel McClean said it was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected".
The majority of the affected staff will be in non-customer facing roles and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told.
VMO2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts that were first reported by Sky News.
As of 30 June, VMO2's total debt stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts.
Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre.
VMO2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by VMO2's owners.
However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) hasprovisionally found competition concerns in the deal,external, with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from VMO2.
At the time, VMO2 called the BT takeover a "stitch-up", which allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market.
BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover.
On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% afterthe Financial Times reported VMO2 was close to agreeing a deal,externalto use its rival's fibre broadband network.
VMO2 was minded to go ahead with the plans after halting upgrades and expansion of its own infrastructure to ease concerns over its debt pile, the paper reported.
The BBC has been told the deal is very close and that VMO2 is highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Ben King

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
summary: Airbnb hosts must stop asking guests to wash-up or take out bins under rules coming into force in November.
body:
Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests
When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.
Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.
But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.
She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.
Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costs
But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.
The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.
Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."
While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal.
"It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."
Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".
Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay in
During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area.
"I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.
For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".
Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.
While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says.
"If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."
Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.
His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".
Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb...
... but will now list just two in light of the new rules
He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals.
"It's common sense and common decency," he says.
His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according todata from AirROI,external.
Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.
Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.
"Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.
Laura Lewis says it's a matter of "basic respect" to wash dishes and take the bins out
The announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.
Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."
Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system.
"If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."
He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect.
"Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
body:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday,taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market valueafter it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

title: Laura Kuenssberg: Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
summary: The Chancellor has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election.
body:
"One step at a time," says Healey on ending the minimum wage gap between older and younger workers
The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.
In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.
But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.
Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.
In a BBC interviewbroadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?
"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.
It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.
Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.
"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.
"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."
"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."
The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling.
The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come.
The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week.
But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."
Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year."
"But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".
She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.
On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."
Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".
Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference.
"So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

title: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
summary: In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Rachel Reeves says Brexit has made the UK "poorer, weaker and less secure".
body:
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.
At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.
The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.
Inthe Sunday Times,external, Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."
She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".
Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation ofthe youth mobility scheme she has been pushing forsince she was in office.
She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.
In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.
She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she "can't even believe we are reopening" the Brexit debate.
She told BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "This is not something that is needed in order to cut welfare, in order to spend money on defence.
"We are having yet another Westminster bubble argument about the EU when it is time for us to actually start using the opportunities, fix mistakes that have been made and go into the future."
Badenoch added: "I do not want to indulge Andy Burnham's fantasies about redoing the referendum because he doesn't have a plan for what to do today."
Burnham told Badenochduring the most recent session of Prime Minister's Questionsthat he was focused on "getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility".
The next UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.

title: Green Party at 'crossroads', says former co-leader
summary: Adrian Ramsay suggested the party needs to focus on its "core values", including environmental issues.
body:
The Green Party is at a "crossroads" and needs to focus on its "core values", a former party co-leader has told the BBC, weeks after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Adrian Ramsay suggested the Greens need their policies to appeal to a majority of British voters if they want to bring the "environmental changes that we need" and advised against taking an approach that risks being "quite divisive".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski responded by saying there was "no environmental justice without social, racial and economic justice".
The motion, which Polanski did not take part in or vote upon, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
I would not have voted for Zionism motion, Polanski says
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month.
It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.
Israel's foreign ministry said it hadbanned Polanski, who is Jewish, from entering the country.
TheEquality and Human Rights Commission also wroteto the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.
Labour later said it wouldend power-sharing agreementswith the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy.
Speaking to Newscast, Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".
The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.
The Fight For The Future Of The Green Party
Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.
He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.
Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.
"One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."
Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".
He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."
Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".
He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".
Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.
He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pairlosing to Polanski in the leadership contest.
Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
summary: The British government has never formally apologised for slavery despite repeated calls from a number of Commonwealth leaders.
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.
He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".
The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.
It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. AsKing Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.
During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities.
On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in apiece for the Guardian,external.
He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation".
He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."
Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference".
The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour.
Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.
He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."
In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said: "I do think we have a duty there and saying sorry is always quite a good thing."
Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing".
"Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."
Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point.
"My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.
Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.
Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
Steve Rosenberg: Inside the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.
Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough.
"The British government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said.
"This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice."
From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.
Burnham is not first UK prime minister to address the issue.
In 2007, the then PM Tony Blairsaid the UK's role in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".
David Cameron ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade in 2015,urging Caribbean countries to "move on" during a visit to Jamaica.
Rishi Sunakdismissed a call for the government to apologise and pay reparations for the UK's historical role in slaveryin 2023 after Bell Ribeiro-Addy asked if he would make a "full and meaningful apology" and "commit to reparatory justice".
Sunak replied with a "no", and said: "Trying to unpick our history is not the right way forward."
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmerruled out compensation for the UK's historical role in the slave trade.
At the time, he said he wanted to focus on the future of the Commonwealth.
Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.
As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.
The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
summary: The home secretary has faced opposition from within the government over plans to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.
She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently  working in social care.
The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.
Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.
In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.
But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.
But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.
The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.
The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.
In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."
"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."
Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.
